paragraphs.heading: What evil actually is
paragraphs.edited: In this first lesson, we want students to really understand what evil is. Evil is the opposite of good. It's the opposite of God. A lot of people will sort of assert that evil is this thing that maybe God created — that maybe God did something where, as part of the whole created universe, there is this force called evil, and it's the opposite of good: good's a thing and evil's a thing. But evil is the absence of good. It's a privation of good. It's sort of the same thing as darkness. We don't have a measurement for darkness; the measurement is light, and darkness is what we call the absence of light.

paragraphs.heading: Evil points to God
paragraphs.edited: So what that leads us to conclude — and this is where the philosophical piece comes in — is that the very fact that evil exists suggests that God exists. Think of it this way. If there is no good, then there is no evil. If there's no God, there's no good. If there's no good, there's no evil. And if there's no good, then there's no evil — which means there's nothing to compare it to. The only way in which we understand what evil is is because we have good, because we can look at evil and say, that's not good.

paragraphs.heading: Small group time
paragraphs.edited: Okay, so, small group time. You're going to get questions, and it's going to get real, real fast. This is the point where students are going to start bringing up probably a load of questions on you, like, well, why does God allow suffering? Why does God allow good people to suffer? Why do bad things happen to good people? And any other variation of the question that basically says, why is there evil and suffering? Some of it you can probably answer as it relates to evil specifically. Some of it you may want to table. But be careful how you table a question. Make sure you write it down — in your leader's guide, your discussion guide, or wherever you have to — so you can come back to it and so you don't ignore the question.
